(`"2"` = mechanism directly observed empirically; `"1"` = documented statistical/descriptive association; `"0"` = inferred only by authors).

effect_estimate.comment: Note slight rounding differences in the paper between Abstract (overall 47%, 95% CI: 45%-49%; range 18% [95% CI: 14%-23%] to 76% [95% CI: 70%-81%]) and Results/Table 1 (overall 47%, 95% CI: 44%-49%, weighted 46.7%; range 19% [95% CI: 15%-24%] in Lukanga WSC to 77% [95% CI: 71%-82%] in Kafubu WSC), and p-value thresholds between text p. 14 and Table 4 footnotes on p. 15.
effect_estimate.value: Overall, 47% (95% CI: 44%, 49%; unweighted n = 1,398/3,047) of urban/peri-urban piped-water households reported water being unavailable for >=1 full day in the preceding fortnight, varying across regulated provider coverage areas (PCAs) from 19% (95% CI: 15%, 24%) in Lukanga WSC to 77% (95% CI: 71%, 82%) in Kafubu WSC. In two-level multilevel logistic regression (n = 3,047 households in 177 clusters), home ownership (at least partly owning vs not owning) was associated with higher odds of interruption in Model 1 (OR = 1.31, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01) and Model 2 (OR = 1.32, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01). Controlling for household factors (Model 1, ref: Lusaka WSC), interruption odds differed markedly across utility service areas: Kafubu WSC OR = 8.02 (SE = 3.40, p < 0.01), Mulongo WSC OR = 3.77 (SE = 1.85, p < 0.05), Luapula WSC OR = 2.89 (SE = 1.45, p < 0.05), Chambeshi WSC OR = 2.43 (SE = 0.94, p < 0.05), Nkana WSC OR = 2.24 (SE = 0.90, p < 0.10), and Lukanga WSC OR = 0.36 (SE = 0.15, p < 0.05). Using a neighbour's tap vs piped into dwelling had OR = 1.33 (SE = 0.21, p < 0.10) in Model 2. At provider level (Model 2), GDP per capita reduced interruption odds (OR = 0.51 per $1,000, SE = 0.11, p < 0.01), while regulator-reported LPCD had no main effect (OR = 1.01, SE = 0.01, NS) but interacted with middle neighbourhood wealth (OR = 0.97, SE = 0.01, p < 0.05) and provider GDP per capita (OR = 1.02, SE = 0.01, p < 0.01).
